title: Trigonometric Functions
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: A trigonometric ratio such as sine, cosine, or tangent begins as a relationship between the sides of a right triangle. But trigonometry becomes much more powerful when we stop thinking of these ratios only as triangle calculations and recognize them as functions. A trigonometric function takes an angle as its input and produces a number as its output. This viewpoint allows us to study trigonometric quantities for every real angle, understand their domain and range, and eventually study their graphs, periodic behavior, and applications.

content.text: In a right triangle, we learned that an angle can determine ratios between the sides. For example, for an angle \(\theta\), sine is defined by \(\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), cosine by \(\cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), and tangent by \(\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\).

The important observation is that these ratios depend on the angle, not on the particular size of the triangle. If two right triangles contain the same acute angle, they are similar, so their corresponding side lengths have the same proportions. Therefore, a particular angle is associated with a particular trigonometric value.

This gives us the idea of a function. A function is a rule that assigns an output to an input. In a trigonometric function, the input is an angle and the output is the corresponding trigonometric value.

For example, when we write \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), we can interpret this as saying that the sine function takes the angle \(30^\circ\) as its input and produces \(\frac{1}{2}\) as its output.

The function viewpoint is more general than simply calculating a side of a triangle. Instead of asking only for the missing side of one triangle, we can ask what value the function produces for any angle.

sections.title: Angle as Input and Ratio as Output

content.text: A useful way to understand a trigonometric function is to imagine a machine. You give the machine an angle, and the function produces a number. For sine, the machine is called the sine function. For cosine, it is the cosine function. For tangent, it is the tangent function.
For example, the sine function gives \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\sin 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), and \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\). The angle is the input and the resulting number is the output.

The output is not necessarily a side length. It is a dimensionless ratio. This is important because the same angle can occur in triangles of many different sizes, but the corresponding trigonometric ratio remains the same.

Once trigonometric ratios are treated as functions, we can also consider angles outside the range of a single right triangle. Using the coordinate-plane definition of trigonometric functions, sine, cosine, and tangent can be associated with positive, negative, and larger angles.
This is the bridge between elementary right-triangle trigonometry and the broader study of trigonometric functions.

Function notation tells us explicitly which input is being given to a function. For ordinary functions, we might write \(f(x)\). In trigonometry, we commonly use \(\sin(x)\), \(\cos(x)\), and \(\tan(x)\).

The expression \(\sin(x)\) means the value produced by the sine function when the input is \(x\). Similarly, \(\cos(x)\) means the value produced by cosine for input \(x\), and \(\tan(x)\) means the value produced by tangent for input \(x\).
The parentheses do not mean multiplication. In \(\sin(x)\), the \(x\) is the input of the sine function.
For example, \(\sin(30^\circ)\) and \(\sin 30^\circ\) mean the same thing. Both represent the sine of an angle measuring \(30^\circ\).

It is also important to distinguish the function from its value. \(\sin(x)\) refers to the sine function applied to an input \(x\), while \(\sin(30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}\) is a particular output of that function.
Sine is one of the three core trigonometric functions. The detailed sine graph, transformations, and behavior are developed in sine-function; this overview only establishes its place in the family.

Cosine is one of the three core trigonometric functions. The detailed cosine graph, transformations, and behavior are developed in cosine-function; this overview only establishes its place in the family.

Tangent is the third core trigonometric function. Its detailed domain, asymptotes, graph, period, and behavior are developed in tangent-function; this overview only establishes its place in the family.

The three basic trigonometric functions are closely connected. In a right triangle, sine compares opposite to hypotenuse, cosine compares adjacent to hypotenuse, and tangent compares opposite to adjacent.
The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA summarizes these three definitions: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, and Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent.
There is also an algebraic relationship between the functions: \(\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), whenever \(\cos\theta \neq 0\).

These functions should not be thought of as three unrelated rules. They describe different relationships associated with the same angle. Knowing one ratio and additional information about the angle can often help determine another.
For example, at \(45^\circ\), we know \(\sin45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) and \(\cos45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). Therefore, \(\tan45^\circ = \frac{\sin45^\circ}{\cos45^\circ} = 1\).

sections.title: Domain and Range: The Family-Level View

content.text: Domain asks which angle inputs are allowed; range asks which numerical outputs a trigonometric function can produce.
For this family, sine and cosine accept every real angle and stay between −1 and 1. Tangent accepts every real angle except where cosine is zero, and its range is all real numbers.

The detailed reasons, equations, and graph behavior belong to the dedicated sine-function, cosine-function, and tangent-function lessons. This section provides the comparison students need before moving between those lessons.
Sine is defined for every real angle, so its domain is ℝ. Its output is always between −1 and 1 because sine is the vertical coordinate of a unit-circle point.
The detailed unit-circle explanation and graph behavior are developed in sine-function; this section keeps only the family-level domain/range fact needed for comparison.
Cosine is defined for every real angle, so its domain is ℝ. Its output is always between −1 and 1 because cosine is the horizontal coordinate of a unit-circle point.
The detailed unit-circle explanation and graph behavior are developed in cosine-function; this section keeps only the family-level domain/range fact needed for comparison.
Tangent is defined wherever cosine is nonzero. In radians its excluded inputs are x = π/2 + kπ, k ∈ ℤ. Its range is ℝ.
The detailed denominator reasoning, asymptotes, periodicity, and graph behavior belong to tangent-function; this section keeps only the comparison facts needed here.

sections.title: Why Tangent Has a Restricted Domain

content.text: The essential reason is division: tan x = sin x / cos x, so cosine cannot be zero.

The dedicated tangent-function lesson develops the geometry and graph consequences of this restriction. Here the goal is only to understand why tangent differs from sine and cosine at the domain level.

sections.title: Domain and Range of Secant, Cosecant and Cotangent

content.text: The three reciprocal functions were introduced as ratios in reciprocal-trigonometric-ratios. Their full function-level domains, ranges, periods, asymptotes, and graphs are developed in reciprocal-trigonometric-functions. Here they are included only to complete the six-function family overview.

sections.title: Angles as Inputs: Degrees and Radians

content.text: An angle can be measured using degrees or radians. Both units describe the same geometric angle, but they use different numerical measurements.
A complete revolution is \(360^\circ\), which is equivalent to \(2\pi\) radians. A half revolution is \(180^\circ = \pi\) radians, and a quarter revolution is \(90^\circ = \frac{\pi}{2}\) radians.
The trigonometric functions themselves do not fundamentally change when we switch units. Only the numerical representation of the input angle changes.
For example, \(\sin90^\circ = 1\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1\). These are the same angle expressed in different units.

When working with a calculator, the angle mode matters. If the calculator is set to degree mode, entering \(\sin(30)\) means the sine of \(30^\circ\). In radian mode, it means the sine of \(30\) radians. These are completely different angles.
Example 1: Compare the domain and range of sine, cosine, and tangent. Sine and cosine have domain ℝ and range [−1,1]. Tangent excludes x = π/2 + kπ and has range ℝ.

Example 2: Explain why tan x can exceed 1 while sin x and cos x cannot. Sine and cosine are coordinates on the unit circle, so they stay in [−1,1]. Tangent is a quotient of those coordinates and can become arbitrarily large when cosine is close to zero.
Example 3: Explain why tan x is undefined at π/2. At that angle cos x = 0, so tan x would require division by zero.

sections.title: A Visual Way to Think About Trigonometric Functions

content.text: Imagine a point moving around a circle centered at the origin. As the point rotates, its horizontal and vertical coordinates continuously change.

On a unit circle, the point corresponding to an angle \(\theta\) has coordinates \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). Therefore, cosine tells us the horizontal position of the point and sine tells us the vertical position.
Tangent can then be understood as the ratio of the vertical coordinate to the horizontal coordinate: \(\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), whenever the horizontal coordinate is not zero.

This moving-point picture explains several properties at once. Sine and cosine stay between \(-1\) and \(1\) because the coordinates of a point on the unit circle cannot leave that interval. Tangent becomes undefined when the horizontal coordinate becomes zero.

A useful visualization for the learning interface would show a rotating radius on a unit circle, display the current angle, and dynamically show the values of \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\), and \(\tan\theta\).

sections.title: Connecting This Topic to Earlier Ideas

content.text: This concept gathers earlier ideas into one function framework. For detailed treatments, follow the dedicated sine-function, cosine-function, tangent-function, and reciprocal-trigonometric-functions concepts rather than repeating those lessons here.
Mistake 1: Assuming all trigonometric functions have the same domain. Tangent has excluded inputs; sine and cosine do not.
Mistake 2: Assuming all trigonometric functions have outputs only between −1 and 1. That is true for sine and cosine, not tangent.
Mistake 3: Relearning the full graph of a function from this overview. Use the dedicated function lesson when detailed graph behavior is required.

The central idea of this chapter is that trigonometric ratios can be viewed as functions. Instead of thinking only about a particular triangle, we can think of an angle as an input and a trigonometric value as an output.

The three fundamental functions are \(\sin x\), \(\cos x\), and \(\tan x\). Sine and cosine are defined for every real input and have range \([-1,1]\). Tangent is undefined when cosine is zero and has range \(\mathbb{R}\).

The reciprocal functions extend the same structure: \(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\), \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\), and \(\cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}\). Their domain restrictions arise naturally from division by zero.

The most important conceptual transition is from 'a ratio in a triangle' to 'a function whose input is an angle.' Once this transition is understood, trigonometry becomes a study of functions with predictable values, restrictions, symmetries, and eventually graphs.

formulas.name: Sine
formulas.explanation: For an acute angle in a right triangle, sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse.

formulas.name: Cosine
formulas.explanation: For an acute angle in a right triangle, cosine is the ratio of the side adjacent to the angle to the hypotenuse.

formulas.name: Tangent
formulas.explanation: For an acute angle in a right triangle, tangent is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the side adjacent to it.

formulas.name: Tangent in Terms of Sine and Cosine
formulas.explanation: Tangent can be expressed as sine divided by cosine whenever cosine is nonzero.

formulas.name: Sine Domain and Range
formulas.explanation: Sine is defined for every real angle, and its output always lies between -1 and 1.

formulas.name: Cosine Domain and Range
formulas.explanation: Cosine is defined for every real angle, and its output always lies between -1 and 1.

formulas.name: Tangent Domain
formulas.explanation: Tangent is undefined whenever cosine is zero, which occurs at odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

formulas.name: Tangent Range
formulas.explanation: Tangent can produce every real number, so it has no upper or lower bound.

formulas.name: Secant
formulas.explanation: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine and is undefined wherever cosine is zero.

formulas.name: Cosecant
formulas.explanation: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine and is undefined wherever sine is zero.

formulas.name: Cotangent
formulas.explanation: Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent and can also be written as cosine divided by sine.

formulas.name: Degrees and Radians
formulas.explanation: This is the fundamental conversion relationship between degree and radian measures.

examples.question: Evaluate \(\sin30^\circ\).
examples.solution: From the exact trigonometric values, \(\sin30^\circ=\frac{1}{2}\). Therefore, the sine function takes \(30^\circ\) as its input and produces \(\frac{1}{2}\) as its output.

examples.question: Is \(\tan90^\circ\) defined?
examples.solution: No. Since \(\cos90^\circ=0\), we have \(\tan90^\circ=\frac{\sin90^\circ}{\cos90^\circ}=\frac{1}{0}\). Division by zero is undefined, so \(\tan90^\circ\) is undefined.

examples.question: What is the range of \(\sin x\)?
examples.solution: On the unit circle, sine represents the vertical coordinate of a point. A point on the unit circle cannot have a vertical coordinate below \(-1\) or above \(1\). Both values occur, so the range is \([-1,1]\).

examples.question: What is the range of \(\cos x\)?
examples.solution: Cosine represents the horizontal coordinate of a point on the unit circle. That coordinate always lies between \(-1\) and \(1\), and both endpoints occur. Therefore, the range is \([-1,1]\).

examples.question: What is the range of \(\tan x\)?
examples.solution: Tangent is not bounded above or below. It can produce any real number. Therefore, the range is \(\mathbb{R}\).

examples.question: Evaluate \(\sec60^\circ\).
examples.solution: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine. Since \(\cos60^\circ=\frac{1}{2}\), \(\sec60^\circ=\frac{1}{1/2}=2\).

examples.question: Evaluate \(\csc30^\circ\).
examples.solution: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine. Since \(\sin30^\circ=\frac{1}{2}\), \(\csc30^\circ=\frac{1}{1/2}=2\).

examples.question: Evaluate \(\cot45^\circ\).
examples.solution: Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent. Since \(\tan45^\circ=1\), \(\cot45^\circ=\frac{1}{1}=1\).

examples.question: Explain why \(\sec90^\circ\) is undefined.
examples.solution: Since \(\sec\theta=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\) and \(\cos90^\circ=0\), we get \(\sec90^\circ=\frac{1}{0}\). Division by zero is undefined, so \(\sec90^\circ\) is undefined.

key_ideas: A function assigns an output to an input.
A trigonometric function takes an angle as its input and produces a numerical value as its output.
Sine, cosine, and tangent originate from ratios of sides in right triangles.
Similar triangles explain why a fixed angle produces a fixed trigonometric ratio.
The notation \(\sin(x)\), \(\cos(x)\), and \(\tan(x)\) describes functions applied to an input.
Sine and cosine can be defined for every real angle.
The range of sine is \([-1,1]\).
The range of cosine is \([-1,1]\).
Tangent is defined using sine divided by cosine.
Tangent is undefined whenever cosine is zero.
The range of tangent is all real numbers.
A trigonometric function can use degrees or radians as the unit for its angle input.
On the unit circle, cosine corresponds to the x-coordinate.
On the unit circle, sine corresponds to the y-coordinate.
Tangent can be viewed as the ratio of the vertical coordinate to the horizontal coordinate.
The reciprocal functions are secant, cosecant, and cotangent.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine.
Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent.
Division by zero creates domain restrictions for reciprocal trigonometric functions.
Sine and cosine are bounded, while tangent is unbounded.
An undefined trigonometric value is not the same thing as an infinitely large value.
The function viewpoint is the bridge from triangle-based trigonometry to the study of trigonometric graphs.
Domain describes the allowed inputs of a function.
Range describes the possible outputs of a function.
The exact values learned earlier become specific input-output examples of trigonometric functions.
misconceptions: A trigonometric function output is a side length.
Sine and cosine can be larger than 1.
Tangent must also lie between -1 and 1.
An undefined value and infinity mean the same thing.
The domain of every trigonometric function is all real numbers.
Secant, cosecant, and cotangent have the same domains as their original functions.
Changing from degrees to radians changes the actual geometric angle rather than only its numerical representation.
The reciprocal of a trigonometric function is the same thing as an inverse trigonometric function.
Right-triangle definitions alone are sufficient for every possible angle.
A function can have only positive outputs.
If two triangles have different side lengths, their trigonometric ratios must be different even when the angle is the same.
